content: The Global Competency and Outcomes Framework for Universal Health Coverage (UHC) identifies six essential domains of health worker competencies: people-centeredness, decision-making, communication, collaboration, evidence-informed practice, and personal conduct. These competencies are highly relevant to adolescent health care and are contextualized in the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Core Competencies for Adolescent Health and Development for Primary Care Providers. All health workers in settings frequented by adolescents, such as hospitals, primary care facilities, and pharmacies, should develop these competencies. The WHO framework outlines specific domains for adolescent health care competencies. These include understanding basic concepts of adolescent health and development, effective communication, situational clinical care, adherence to laws and policies (e.g., informed consent, confidentiality, and privacy), and compliance with quality standards for adolescent-friendly care. Despite growing awareness of adolescent health needs, gaps remain in the quality of adolescent health education within national pediatric training programs. This highlights the inadequacy of current training and the need for a stronger focus on adolescent health within pediatrics to prepare the workforce for evolving disease burdens across childhood and adolescence. Core competencies in adolescent health should be integrated into both pre-service and in-service education to promote lifelong learning. However, many countries lack sustainable systems for continuous professional education, underscoring the importance of improving the structure, content, and quality of adolescent health curricula. One critical step toward building a competent workforce in adolescent health is mandating competency-based education in pre-service and postgraduate training for key professions, including nursing, midwifery, primary care, mental health, and sexual and reproductive health (SRH) specialists. WHO’s Core Competencies in Adolescent Health and Development for Primary Care Providers was developed to support countries in creating an adolescent-competent workforce. In Mauritius, adolescents represent 6% of the population. Surveys have shown the need to prioritize their specific health needs and address risky behaviors through comprehensive actions targeting barriers such as poverty, limited access to adolescent-friendly services, conservative social norms, and discrimination. Recognizing the importance of adolescents in society, the Ministry of Health and Wellness (MOHW) is leading the development of the National Strategy for Adolescent Health (2023–2027) with input from various ministries and community engagement. The MOHW has also extended the pediatric age limit from 12 to 16 years and invested in adolescent health training for pediatricians and policymakers. In April 2023, WHO supported a master training program to equip health providers with skills to address adolescents' multifaceted needs, including mental health, SRH, non-communicable disease prevention, and substance use. Ethiopia, with a rapidly growing youth population, has prioritized adolescent health in its Health Sector Transformation Plan and aims to meet Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030. The National Adolescent and Youth Health Strategy (2016–2020) emphasized strengthening pre-service training for adolescent health practitioners. Needs assessments revealed that a lack of competent providers compromises adolescents' access to health services. Stakeholders identified the need for comprehensive pre-service training to address competency gaps. Ethiopia’s Adolescent Health and Development Curriculum was designed to develop advanced competencies in areas such as adolescent development, effective communication, mental health assessment, prevention of risky behaviors, gender-transformative interventions, and advocacy for adolescents' health rights. The curriculum is now being used to define competencies for in-service training, although its formal implementation has been delayed. In Uganda, adolescent medicine was not a recognized specialty until 2016. Since then, significant progress has been made, including the introduction of a six-week adolescent health course for postgraduate pediatric trainees. This course includes lectures, practical training, and outreach activities, enabling trainees to become champions for adolescent health care. Makerere University has also developed a comprehensive training program for faculty and resource persons to deliver updated content using interactive teaching techniques. Over 400 students, including undergraduates and postgraduates, have received training in adolescent health since 2019. Ghana has implemented a digital solution to monitor the quality of adolescent health care services. Using WHO’s web-based platform, six facilities piloted the system, collecting data on care quality from over 3,000 adolescents and health staff. The platform has improved communication, professional competencies, and the standardization of tools and materials. Ghana has since scaled up the platform’s use, with plans to enhance data management, provide learning materials, and train service providers in its application. Global initiatives emphasize the importance of integrating adolescent-specific considerations into health care policies and practices. Strategies include developing national quality standards, implementing competency-based training, and using digital tools to improve service delivery. By addressing these challenges, countries can build a competent workforce and improve the quality of care for adolescents, aligning with the broader goals of Universal Health Coverage and the SDGs.
